answer: Social. In the Social discipline, both original and replication studies primarily used student subjects: 82.04% of originals (subjects.o == 'students') and 78.44% of replications (subjects.r == 'students') over the full 927-row table — the discipline closest to the question's stated 82.4% / 80.9%. payload.hypothesis: The Social domain (discipline = Social) is where both original and replication studies primarily used student subjects: originals 82.0% and replications 78.4% of rows (computed over the full 927-row table, missing subject values treated as not-student; excluding the single missing row gives 82.2%/78.6%, and study-level dedup by id gives 83.8%/81.1%), the closest match to the stated 82.4% (original) and 80.9% (replication) — the small gap likely reflecting a data-version or rounding difference. No other discipline (Cognitive: 71.4%/83.8%; Economics: 94.4%/100.0%) or project (best: rpp 80.4%/76.3%) fits both figures.
payload.workflow: Single pandas script (analysis/student_subjects_domain.py): load the study heterogeneity CSV (927 rows × 57 cols; no join with the second CSV, which lacks subjects/discipline fields); compute per-discipline shares of subjects.o=='students' and subjects.r=='students' over all rows with the one missing-subjects row (NaN in both) treated as not-student; verify Social is closest to the stated 82.4%/80.9% targets; run two sensitivity checks (excluding the missing row; dedup to first row per id since rows are study×effect with 786 duplicated ids); cross-check by project field. 'drop' and 'aggregated' meta-regression flags were intentionally not used as filters.
